questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: Georgia intangible recording tax applies to
questions.text: Georgia's intangible recording tax is imposed on:

answers.text: new mortgage loans secured by real property in Georgia
the gross sale price of every residential property sold in the state
prepayment of any existing mortgage within the first three years
interest income earned by Georgia-licensed mortgage lenders

explanations.a: Under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-61, Georgia's intangible recording tax is levied on the face amount of long-term notes (mortgages) secured by real property located in Georgia, paid when the security instrument is recorded.
explanations.b: The sale price is subject to the real estate transfer tax, not the intangible recording tax.
explanations.c: Prepayment of an existing mortgage does not trigger a new intangible recording tax; only recording a new security instrument does.
explanations.d: Lender interest income is subject to federal and state income tax, not the intangible recording tax.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: intangible recording tax rate per thousand
questions.text: The rate of Georgia's intangible recording tax on a new mortgage is:

answers.text: $1.00 per $1,000 of the loan amount
$3.00 per $1,000 of the loan amount ($1.50 per $500)
$10.00 per $1,000 of the loan amount
1% of the total loan amount

explanations.a: $1.00 per $1,000 is the rate for Georgia's real estate transfer tax on deeds, not the intangible recording tax on mortgages.
explanations.b: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-61 sets the intangible recording tax at $1.50 per $500 of the principal amount of the note, which equals $3.00 per $1,000.
explanations.c: $10.00 per $1,000 would be ten times the actual rate and would make Georgia's tax among the highest in the nation.
explanations.d: 1% of the loan amount would be $3.33 per $1,000 at the $200,000 level and does not match the statutory formula of $1.50 per $500.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: intangible recording tax dollar calculation
questions.text: A Georgia buyer obtains a $200,000 mortgage to purchase a home. What is the intangible recording tax due at closing?

explanations.a: $200 would result from applying $1/$1,000 (the transfer tax rate) instead of the mortgage intangible rate.
explanations.b: $300 would result from applying $1.50 per $1,000 — only half the statutory rate — instead of the full $3.00 per $1,000.
explanations.c: Intangible recording tax = $200,000 ÷ $1,000 × $3.00 = $600. ($200 thousand × $3 per thousand = $600.)
explanations.d: $1,000 would result from applying $5/$1,000, which exceeds the statutory rate.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: Georgia real estate transfer tax paid by seller
questions.text: In Georgia, the real estate transfer tax imposed when a deed is recorded is typically paid by:

answers.text: the buyer, as part of the total loan closing costs
both buyer and seller equally as a shared closing cost
the closing attorney, who collects from the title insurance underwriter
the seller (grantor), based on the amount of consideration received

explanations.a: The real estate transfer tax is the seller's obligation under Georgia law, not the buyer's.
explanations.b: Georgia law places the transfer tax obligation on the grantor (seller); it is not split.
explanations.c: The closing attorney collects and remits the tax, but it is charged to the seller's proceeds, not funded by the title insurer.
explanations.d: Under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1, the real estate transfer tax is imposed on the grantor (seller) and is calculated at $1.00 per $1,000 of the purchase price.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: Georgia transfer tax rate per thousand
questions.text: Georgia's real estate transfer tax is calculated at:

answers.text: $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price
$1.00 per $1,000 of the sale price
$5.00 per $1,000 of the sale price
2% of the sale price

explanations.a: $3.00 per $1,000 is the rate for Georgia's intangible recording tax on mortgages, not the transfer tax on deeds.
explanations.b: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1 imposes a transfer tax of $1.00 per $1,000 (or $0.10 per $100) of the purchase price.
explanations.c: $5.00 per $1,000 significantly overstates the statutory rate.
explanations.d: 2% of the sale price would be $20 per $1,000, far above the statutory $1 per $1,000.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: transfer tax dollar calculation on sale
questions.text: A Georgia home sells for $250,000. What is the real estate transfer tax owed by the seller at closing?

explanations.a: $25 would result from applying $0.10 per $1,000 instead of $1.00 per $1,000.
explanations.b: $100 results from applying the $1/$1,000 rate to only $100,000 of the price.
explanations.d: $750 would result from applying a $3/$1,000 rate — the intangible recording tax rate — to the purchase price.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: Georgia property taxes paid in arrears
questions.text: In Georgia, ad valorem (property) taxes are:

answers.text: paid in advance at the beginning of each calendar year
collected monthly by the state government through the escrow account
levied by the federal government and remitted to Georgia counties
paid in arrears, meaning taxes for the current year are collected after the year ends

explanations.a: Georgia property taxes are due and payable in arrears, not in advance at the beginning of the year.
explanations.b: Escrow accounts collect estimates of taxes monthly for later payment to the taxing authority; the state government does not collect taxes directly from escrow.
explanations.c: Property taxes are levied by local county and city governments, not the federal government.
explanations.d: Georgia ad valorem taxes are billed and paid in arrears — typically in the fall for the current calendar year — which means at a mid-year closing the seller owes a proration for the period they owned the property.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: Loan Estimate three business days of application
questions.text: Under the TRID rules applicable to Georgia mortgage loans, a lender must deliver the Loan Estimate to the borrower within:

answers.text: three business days of receiving the borrower's completed loan application
five business days of the property appraisal being completed
10 business days after the underwriter issues a conditional approval
24 hours of the buyer signing the purchase and sale agreement

explanations.a: TRID (TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure) rules require lenders to provide the Loan Estimate within three business days of receiving a completed loan application from the borrower.
explanations.b: The Loan Estimate is triggered by the application, not by the appraisal; there is no five-business-day appraisal rule for the LE.
explanations.c: Underwriter approval comes after the LE is issued; the LE timeline is tied to application, not approval.
explanations.d: The purchase contract signing does not trigger the Loan Estimate; the loan application triggers it.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: Closing Disclosure three business days before closing
questions.text: Under TRID rules, the Closing Disclosure must be provided to the buyer at least:

answers.text: 10 business days before the scheduled closing date
24 hours before the scheduled closing date
three business days before the scheduled closing date
30 calendar days before the scheduled closing date

explanations.a: 10 business days before closing is the Loan Estimate waiting period, not the Closing Disclosure waiting period.
explanations.b: 24 hours is insufficient; TRID mandates at least three business days before closing.
explanations.c: TRID requires lenders to deliver the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before consummation, giving borrowers time to review final terms.
explanations.d: 30 calendar days is not the Closing Disclosure requirement; it significantly exceeds the actual waiting period.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: revised Closing Disclosure new three-day wait
questions.text: If a lender issues a revised Closing Disclosure reflecting an APR increase above the permitted tolerance threshold, the lender must:

answers.text: proceed to closing immediately because TRID tolerances are self-correcting
send the revised CD and close within 24 hours provided the borrower verbally approves
allow the borrower to waive the new waiting period by signing a waiver form
issue the revised Closing Disclosure and wait an additional three business days before closing

explanations.a: A material change such as an APR increase above tolerance is not self-correcting; it restarts the three-business-day clock.
explanations.b: A verbal approval does not substitute for the statutory waiting period; the borrower must receive and have time to review the revised CD.
explanations.c: Borrowers may waive the waiting period only in limited circumstances involving a bona fide personal financial emergency, not simply for convenience.
explanations.d: TRID provides that significant changes to the Closing Disclosure — including APR increases beyond the allowed tolerance — trigger a new three-business-day waiting period before the loan can close.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: PMI not required at 80 percent LTV
questions.text: A buyer making a 20% down payment on a conventional mortgage loan would generally NOT be required to pay:

answers.text: private mortgage insurance (PMI)
prepaid interest from the closing date to the end of the month
the Georgia intangible recording tax on the new mortgage
the lender's origination fee

explanations.a: PMI is required on conventional loans only when the LTV exceeds 80%; a 20% down payment produces exactly 80% LTV, below the PMI trigger.
explanations.b: Prepaid interest from the closing date to month-end is a standard closing cost regardless of down payment size.
explanations.c: The Georgia intangible recording tax applies to any new mortgage loan secured by Georgia real estate; the down payment amount does not affect it.
explanations.d: Lender origination fees are charged based on the loan amount and terms, not the size of the down payment.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: attorney closing state unauthorized practice of law
questions.text: Georgia requires a licensed attorney to conduct real estate closings primarily because:

answers.text: mortgage lenders require an attorney to guarantee title accuracy
preparing and supervising closing documents constitutes the practice of law under Georgia's unauthorized practice of law doctrine
GREC regulations mandate attorney supervision of all licensed real estate transactions
Georgia's Real Estate License Act prohibits licensees from handling closing funds

explanations.a: Lenders desire title insurance rather than an attorney guarantee; the attorney requirement stems from the practice-of-law doctrine, not lender preference.
explanations.b: Georgia courts and the State Bar have determined that the preparation and oversight of closing documents — including deeds and title opinion — constitutes the practice of law, so a licensed Georgia attorney must conduct or supervise the closing.
explanations.c: GREC regulates real estate licensees but does not mandate attorney supervision; the basis is the unauthorized practice of law doctrine enforced by the State Bar.
explanations.d: Real estate licensees may hold client funds in trust accounts; the attorney requirement is based on the legal nature of document preparation, not fund handling.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: prepaid interest closing cost coverage period
questions.text: The prepaid interest collected from a buyer at a Georgia mortgage closing covers:

answers.text: interest owed from the first scheduled payment date back to the loan origination
two months of interest collected to build a lender reserve for missed payments
interest charged for the first full calendar month of the loan term
interest accrued from the closing date through the end of the month in which closing occurs

explanations.a: Prepaid interest does not cover a retrospective period; it covers the days from closing to the end of the current month.
explanations.b: A reserve for missed payments describes a different escrow mechanism, not prepaid interest.
explanations.c: The first full month's interest is included in the first regular mortgage payment, not at closing.
explanations.d: Lenders collect prepaid interest at closing to cover the days from the closing date through the end of that month, so the first regular payment (beginning on the first of the following month) covers a full month.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: earnest money credited toward purchase price
questions.text: At a Georgia real estate closing, the earnest money previously deposited by the buyer is:

answers.text: credited toward the buyer's total funds needed to close
paid directly to the listing broker as partial commission
returned in full to the buyer as a reward for completing the transaction
held in reserve by the closing attorney for 30 days after closing in case of post-closing claims

explanations.a: The earnest money, held in trust during the transaction, is credited toward the buyer's total funds required to close, reducing the cash the buyer must bring to the closing table.
explanations.b: Commission is paid from the seller's proceeds; earnest money belongs to the transaction and is credited to the buyer, not paid to the broker.
explanations.c: Earnest money is applied to the purchase price, not returned; it was consideration for the seller's taking the property off the market.
explanations.d: Upon a successful closing, earnest money is released and credited at closing; there is no 30-day post-closing hold.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: property tax proration reason Georgia arrears
questions.text: In a Georgia real estate closing, property taxes are prorated between buyer and seller because:

answers.text: state law requires the closing attorney to collect all unpaid taxes before recording the deed
Georgia taxes are paid in arrears and must be allocated based on each party's days of ownership during the tax year
the buyer's lender requires the seller to clear all tax obligations before funding the loan
GREC regulations require tax proration to prevent disputes after closing

explanations.a: The closing attorney facilitates the proration but does not separately collect taxes from the state; the proration is a financial adjustment between buyer and seller.
explanations.b: Because Georgia property taxes are billed and paid in arrears, the seller typically owes taxes for the portion of the year they owned the property, and the buyer receives a credit for that amount to pay the bill when it comes due.
explanations.c: The lender requires clear title, not necessarily a proration; the proration is a contract and accounting matter between the parties.
explanations.d: Tax proration is a standard real estate practice that predates GREC regulations; it flows from how taxes are assessed and when they are paid.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: tax proration seller credit calculation
questions.text: A Georgia home closes on September 30. Annual property taxes of $3,600 are unpaid. Using a 360-day banker's year, how much does the seller owe the buyer as a tax proration?

explanations.a: $900 represents only 3 months of taxes; the seller owned the property for 9 months (January through September).
explanations.b: $1,800 represents 6 months; the seller is responsible for 9 months, not 6.
explanations.c: Monthly tax = $3,600 ÷ 12 = $300. Seller's 9 months (Jan–Sep) = $300 × 9 = $2,700. The seller is debited and the buyer is credited $2,700 at closing.
explanations.d: $3,600 is the full annual tax; only the seller's 9-month share is prorated.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: real estate commission paid from seller proceeds
questions.text: At a Georgia real estate closing, the real estate brokerage commission is customarily paid by:

answers.text: the seller from the sale proceeds
the buyer as an additional closing cost on the Closing Disclosure
the mortgage lender as a closing cost rolled into the loan balance
both parties in equal shares as a negotiated line item

explanations.a: The real estate commission is a seller obligation under the listing agreement and is paid from the seller's proceeds at closing.
explanations.b: In a traditional transaction, the buyer does not pay the commission directly; it is a debit on the seller's settlement statement.
explanations.c: Lenders do not fund real estate commissions; the loan proceeds go to pay off the seller's mortgage and deliver net cash to the seller.
explanations.d: Commission is the seller's obligation under the listing contract; it is not customarily split equally with the buyer.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: lender title insurance required at closing
questions.text: In a Georgia residential purchase involving a mortgage loan, a lender's title insurance policy is:

answers.text: optional and purchased only at the borrower's specific written request
typically required by the mortgage lender as a condition of making the loan
automatically included as part of the Georgia real estate transfer tax
issued by GREC's title guarantee program for all licensee-assisted closings

explanations.a: A lender's policy is not optional in most financed transactions; lenders require it to protect their security interest.
explanations.b: Virtually all mortgage lenders require a lender's title insurance policy as a condition of making the loan, because it protects the lender's interest if a title defect surfaces after closing.
explanations.c: Title insurance is a separate product purchased from a title insurance company; it is not included in any tax.
explanations.d: GREC has no title guarantee program; title insurance is underwritten by private insurance companies.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: seller net proceeds calculation with transfer tax
questions.text: A Georgia seller receives $200,000 from the sale of her home. She pays a 6% commission, the Georgia transfer tax ($1 per $1,000), and has a mortgage payoff of $130,000. What are her approximate net proceeds?

explanations.a: $58,000 results from deducting commission and mortgage but forgetting the transfer tax: $200,000 − $12,000 − $130,000 = $58,000.
explanations.b: $57,600 results from an error in the transfer tax calculation — applying $2/$1,000 ($400) instead of $1/$1,000 ($200).
explanations.d: $70,000 deducts only the mortgage ($200,000 − $130,000) and ignores both the commission and transfer tax.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: buyer closing costs typical Georgia
questions.text: Which of the following closing costs is typically paid by the BUYER in a Georgia residential transaction?

answers.text: real estate transfer tax ($1 per $1,000 of the purchase price)
the seller's real estate brokerage commission
payoff of any existing mortgages on the seller's property
intangible recording tax on the new mortgage ($3 per $1,000 of loan amount)

explanations.a: The real estate transfer tax on the deed is paid by the seller (grantor) under Georgia law.
explanations.b: The brokerage commission is the seller's obligation under the listing agreement.
explanations.c: Payoff of the seller's existing mortgage is the seller's obligation, not the buyer's.
explanations.d: The intangible recording tax on the new mortgage is the buyer's obligation, paid when the security deed is recorded; the buyer is taking on the new loan.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: Closing Disclosure replaced HUD-1
questions.text: The Closing Disclosure (CD) required under TRID replaced which earlier settlement document used at real estate closings?

answers.text: the preliminary title commitment issued by the title company
the Sponsoring Broker Statement required by GREC
the HUD-1 Settlement Statement
the Certification of Accuracy Statement required by AMP

explanations.a: A title commitment is a separate document disclosing title status; it was not replaced by the CD.
explanations.b: The Sponsoring Broker Statement is a licensing form; it has nothing to do with closing disclosures.
explanations.c: TRID, effective October 2015, replaced the HUD-1 Settlement Statement with the Closing Disclosure for most residential mortgage transactions.
explanations.d: The Certification of Accuracy Statement is an AMP licensing document; it is not a settlement disclosure.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: TRID no fees before Loan Estimate reviewed
questions.text: Under TRID, a mortgage lender may NOT collect any fee from the borrower — other than a bona fide credit report fee — until:

answers.text: the appraisal has been ordered and the appraiser's availability confirmed
the underwriter issues a conditional approval of the loan application
the property passes a satisfactory home inspection
the borrower has received and had an opportunity to review the Loan Estimate

explanations.a: Ordering the appraisal is not the event that triggers the fee-collection authorization under TRID.
explanations.b: Underwriter approval comes later in the process; TRID allows limited fees only after the LE is received.
explanations.c: The home inspection is a separate buyer activity; TRID's fee restriction is tied to the Loan Estimate, not the inspection.
explanations.d: TRID prohibits lenders from collecting most fees until the borrower has received the Loan Estimate and indicated intent to proceed, protecting consumers from upfront fee traps.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: PMI automatic cancellation at 78% LTV
questions.text: The Homeowners Protection Act (HPA) requires lenders to automatically cancel private mortgage insurance when the loan balance reaches:

answers.text: 78% of the original purchase price, based on the scheduled amortization
90% of the original purchase price based on the outstanding balance
85% of the current appraised market value
any point at which the borrower's equity exceeds the amount of the original PMI premium paid

explanations.a: Under the Homeowners Protection Act, lenders must automatically terminate PMI when the scheduled mortgage balance reaches 78% of the original purchase price (not current value), based on the amortization schedule.
explanations.b: 90% LTV would mean only 10% equity; PMI cancellation begins well before that point at 80% (borrower request) and 78% (automatic).
explanations.c: The HPA uses the original value, not a new appraisal, for the automatic termination threshold.
explanations.d: PMI cancellation is tied to the LTV ratio, not to cumulative premiums paid.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: prepaid tax proration buyer owes seller
questions.text: A Georgia closing occurs on October 15. The seller already paid the full year's property taxes of $2,400. Using 30-day months, how much does the buyer owe the seller as a proration at closing?

explanations.a: $400 represents only 2 months and would be the buyer's share if the closing were November 30.
explanations.b: Monthly tax = $2,400 ÷ 12 = $200. Buyer owns Oct 16–Dec 31 = 15 days of Oct + 30 days of Nov + 30 days of Dec = 75 days. Daily = $2,400 ÷ 360 = $6.67. Buyer owes: 75 × $6.67 ≈ $500 (or 2.5 months × $200 = $500).
explanations.c: $1,200 represents 6 months — the seller's share, not the buyer's.
explanations.d: $2,000 represents more than 10 months; the buyer owns less than 3 months of the year.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: transfer tax paid by seller at closing
questions.text: In a Georgia real estate closing, the Georgia real estate transfer tax appears on the closing statement as:

answers.text: a debit to the buyer and a credit to the state government
a debit to the seller, reducing the seller's net proceeds
a shared expense debited equally to both buyer and seller
a lender closing cost rolled into the buyer's loan balance

explanations.a: The transfer tax is the seller's obligation, not the buyer's; it appears as a seller debit.
explanations.b: Because Georgia's transfer tax is imposed on the grantor (seller), it is shown as a debit — a charge reducing proceeds — on the seller's side of the closing statement.
explanations.c: The transfer tax is not shared; it is solely a seller obligation under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1.
explanations.d: The transfer tax cannot be financed into the buyer's loan; it is paid from the seller's proceeds at closing.

questions.name: Finance & Closing (Georgia)
questions.keyword: buyer closing costs EXCEPT transfer tax
questions.text: A Georgia buyer's typical closing costs include all of the following EXCEPT:

answers.text: the real estate transfer tax on the deed ($1 per $1,000 of purchase price)
the intangible recording tax on the new mortgage ($3 per $1,000 of loan amount)
prepaid homeowner's insurance for the first year of the policy
the lender's origination fee and any discount points on the loan

explanations.a: The real estate transfer tax is imposed on the seller (grantor); it is not a buyer closing cost.
explanations.b: The intangible recording tax on the new mortgage is the buyer's obligation, paid when the security deed is recorded at closing.
explanations.c: Prepaid homeowner's insurance is a standard buyer closing cost required by most lenders before funding.
explanations.d: Lender origination fees and points are buyer closing costs negotiated with the lender as part of the loan terms.
